Geocentric Models Practice

4.7 Practice

Easy

4E1. In the model definition below, which line is the likelihood?

  1. \(y_{i} ∼ {\sf Normal}(µ, σ)\)
    1. THIS ONE - this is the data we have at hand and want to understand thru the parameters.
  2. \(µ∼Normal(0, 10)\)
  3. \(σ ∼Exponential(1)\)

4E2. In the model definition just above, how many parameters are in the posterior distribution?

  • Two parameters, µ and sigma

4E3. Using the model definition above, write down the appropriate form of Bayes’ theorem that includes the proper likelihood and priors.

\[ Pr(µ,\sigma|y)= \frac{Pr(y|µ,\sigma)(Pr(µ)Pr(\sigma)}{Pr(y)} \]

4E4. In the model definition below, which line is the linear model?

  • \(µ_{i} = \alpha + \beta x_{i}\)

4E5. In the model definition just above, how many parameters are in the posterior distribution?

  • 3 parameters: \(\alpha\) , \(\beta\), \(\sigma\)

Medium

4M1. For the model definition below, simulate observed y values from the prior (not the posterior)

\[ y_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(µ, \sigma) \]

\[ µ \sim {\sf Normal}(0,10) \]

\[ \sigma \sim {\sf Exponential}(1) \]

sim_y <- function(N) {
  sigma <- rexp(N,1)
  mu <- rnorm(N, 0,10)
  y <- rnorm(N, mu, sigma)
  return(y)
}

prior_y <- sim_y(1e4)
dens(prior_y)

4M2. Translate the model just above into a quap formula.

flist <- alist(
    y ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu ~ dnorm(0,10),
    sigma ~ dexp(1))

4M3. Translate the quap model formula below into a mathematical model definition.

\[ y_{i} ~ {\sf Normal}(µ, \sigma) \]

\[ µ_{i} = \alpha + \beta x_{i} \]

\[ \alpha \sim {\sf Normal}(0,10) \]

\[ \beta \sim {\sf Uniform}(0,1) \]

\[ \sigma \sim {\sf Exponential}(1) \]

4M4. A sample of students is measured for height each year for 3 years. After the third year, you want to fit a linear regression predicting height using year as a predictor. Write down the mathematical model definition for this regression, using any variable names and priors you choose. Be prepared to defend your choice of priors.

  • Outcome: height of student

  • Predictor: year (1, 2, or 3)

  • Assumed relationship: height INC linearly over time

\(h_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(\mu, \sigma)\) the likelihood of the height will be normally distributed around the line
\(\mu = \alpha +\beta x_{i}\) Mean will be linear regression function of year (\(x_{i}\) is year 1, 2, or 3 for observation \(i\)).
\(\alpha \sim {\sf Normal}(158, 20)\)

What is the expected height when year = 1?

The intercept will be normally distributed around a mean of around 158 cm. This is just my guess, given the limited information provided: namely, the sample consists of students who can be children as young as 5 years to perhaps 25 years old. The standard deviation should cast a wide range of heights (a bulk of heights around 138-178cm) without being unreasonably lax.
\(\beta \sim {\sf Normal}(5, 2)\)

How many cm do students grow per year?

The slope should reflect that children, adolescents grow at a faster rate than adults, but also keep in mind that the sample may include young adults. I said around 5cm growth, +/-2 cm per year.

The slope should be positive. I could use a Log-Normal to strictly enforce positivity, but Normal(5,2) puts very little mass below zero so it’s reasonable.
\(\sigma \sim {\sf Exponential}(1)\)

How much do individual heights vary around the average line?

Sigma has to be positive, and shouldn’t vary wildly. Exponential(1) has a mean of 1 and a long tail, giving most mass to small values while allowing larger spread if the data demand it. Strictly enforces positive vals.
Code 
par(mfrow=c(2,2))
dens(rnorm(1e4, 158, 20),main = "alpha prior")
dens(rnorm(1e4, 5,2), main = "beta prior")
dens(rlnorm(1e4, 2,0.5), main = "updated beta prior: log-normal")
dens(rexp(1e4,1), main = "sigma prior")

4M5. Now suppose I remind you that every student got taller each year. Does this information lead you to change your choice of priors? How?

Yes, my beta would be Log-Normal(2,0.5)

A Log-Normal(2, 0.5) has a median of \(e^2≈ 7.4\) cm/year, which is realistic, and puts zero mass on negative growth by definition.

4M6. Now suppose I tell you that the variance among heights for students of the same age is never more than 64cm. How does this lead you to revise your priors?

I would change my sigma prior to be uniform: \({\sf Uniform}(0,8)\)

  • WarningDoes not change alpha prior

    The SD in \(\alpha \sim \text{Normal}(158, 20)\) is not about how much students vary from each other. It’s about my own uncertainty in where the mean height is.

Hard

4H1. The weights listed below were recorded in the !Kung census, but heights were not recorded for these individuals. Provide predicted heights and 89% intervals for each of these individuals. That is, fill in the table below, using model-based predictions.

Q4H1_weights <- c(46.95, 43.72, 64.78,32.59,54.63)

# Use link to extract samples from model, calculate the mu values for each weight in list
Q4H1_mu <- link(m4.3, data=data.frame(weight=Q4H1_weights))

# Apply mean to Q4H1_mu (remember: 2 means 'dimension 2' of the matrix Q4H1_mu)
Q4H1_mean <- apply(Q4H1_mu, 2, mean)

4H2. Select out all the rows in the Howell1 data with ages below 18 years of age. If you do it right, you should end up with a new data frame with 192 rows in it.

ImportantCan I use the data summary of the predictor variable to inform my priors?

Priors should encode what you knew before seeing the outcome variable (height), but it’s okay to look at the predictor variable (weight) to understand scale

So glancing at the range of weights to understand your xbar centering is perfectly reasonable. What you want to avoid is looking at the height data and setting a very tight prior directly from it.

d3 <- Howell1[d$age < 18,]
precis(d3)

(a) Fit a linear regression to these data, using quap. Present and interpret the estimates. For every 10 units of increase in weight, how much taller does the model predict a child gets?

# Simulate prior predictive distribution to fuss over the priors!! 
set.seed(2971)
N <- 100
a <- rnorm(N, 100, 10)
b <- rlnorm(N, 0, 0.5)

# Plot the prior predictive simulation
plot(NULL, xlim=range(d3$weight), ylim=c(-100,400),xlab="weight",ylab="height")

abline(h=0, lty=2) # no one is negative height
abline(h=200, lty=2, lwd=0.5) # A pretty tall adult

xbar <- mean(d3$weight)
for (i in 1:N) curve(a[i] + b[i]*(x-xbar), from = min(d3$weight), to=max(d3$weight), add=TRUE, col=col.alpha("black", 0.2))
# Let's find the posterior distribution now 

# xbar is the avg weight of d3
xbar <- mean(d3$weight)

# Fit the linear model
m4.4 <- quap(
  alist(
    height ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + b*(weight - xbar),
    a ~ dnorm(100,10),
    b ~ dlnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dunif(0,10)
  ), data=d3
)

# Interpret your posterior distribution 
precis(m4.4)
            mean         sd       5.5%      94.5%
a     108.283818 0.60767482 107.312636 109.255000
b       2.711239 0.06830794   2.602070   2.820409
sigma   8.435633 0.43037793   7.747806   9.123460
# For every 10 kg weight
cat("\n")
cat("For every 10 kg increase in weight, height increases by:", 10 * coef(m4.4)["b"], "cm \n")

(b) Plot the raw data, with height on the vertical axis and weight on the horizontal axis. Super-impose the MAP (maximum a posteriori estimate) regression line and 89% interval for the mean. Also superimpose the 89% interval for predicted heights.

# Plot raw data 
plot(d3$height ~ d3$weight, col=rangi2, xlab="weight (kg)", ylab="height (cm)")

# extract samples for the linear model's posterior distribution
post <- extract.samples(m4.4)

# get MAP estimate for posterior alpha and beta 
a_map <- mean(post$a)
b_map <- mean(post$b)

# plot MAP regression line 
curve(a_map+ b_map * (x - xbar), add=TRUE)

# superimpose 89% PI for heights
weight.seq <- seq(3,45, by=1)

mu <- link(m4.4, data = data.frame(weight=weight.seq))

#simulate heights with linear model, for each possible weight (1kg seq has 1000 simulated heights)
sim.height <- sim(m4.4, data=list(weight=weight.seq))

height.PI <- apply(sim.height, 2, PI, prob=0.89)
shade(height.PI, weight.seq)

(c) What aspects of the model fit concern you? Describe the kinds of assumptions you would change, if any, to improve the model. You don’t have to write any new code. Just explain what the model appears to be doing a bad job of, and what you hypothesize would be a better model.

Obviously not linear relationship between weight and height. Doesn’t reflect the sharp growth that happens at lighter weights (0-10kg) not the drop off in growth after 35kg. Perhaps a polynomial regression would work better.
